_comment: Saved character configuration for rust-scavenger. Modeled on character-bounds.json (the courier's) — see that file for the long-form rationale on every field below; this copy states only what differs for a ground patroller. THE SCALE LIVES HERE ON PURPOSE (vault A5): a global constant derived from a single regenerable frame means regenerating that frame silently rescales every other animation and moves every measured bound. `npm run assets:build` READS this and never computes it; `node tools/gen/build-assets.mjs rust-scavenger <action> --derive-scale` prints a new one for a human to paste in deliberately.
_scale: Source pixels to game pixels. DERIVED 2026-08-11 (session 6) from `rust-scavenger-walk-r3.mp4` — 240 / 428 = 0.56074766. Pasted by hand from `node tools/gen/build-assets.mjs rust-scavenger walk --derive-scale`, which PRINTS it and never writes it (vault A5: the build reads this number and never computes it). ⚠️ MEASURED FROM A GAIT, NOT A NEUTRAL POSE, and that is not a shortcut — the scavenger patrols continuously and has NO `idle`, deliberately, because a standing pose is a state the sim cannot enter. The twelve walk frames span a mean height of 428 source px with a frame-to-frame spread of 18 px, **4.2%** — against the sentry's 0.3% and the courier's 0.8%. That spread IS the size-pop this scale exists to hold still, and it is larger here because a striding figure genuinely changes height within its cycle; averaging over a full closed cycle (the clip yields exactly 2.0 cycles) is what makes the mean meaningful rather than arbitrary. Re-deriving is mandatory if the walk clip is ever re-shot, and `chase`/`death` must be packed against whatever value stands here, never the reverse. Shares the provenance limitation recorded for the courier and the sentry (Codex C5, docs/qa/phase-05-combat.md limitation 7): the source is a regenerable sheet, not the locked anchor — the anchor cannot supply it, being 3690 square against a 960 square clip.
_renderHeightPx: SCAVENGER_BOX.h (40 sim px, src/sim/enemyPlacement.ts) x RENDER_SCALE (6, src/game/constants.ts) = 240 px = 2.5 tiles. Between the sentry's 192 px and the courier's 288 px on purpose — three distinct silhouette heights (src/sim/enemyPlacement.ts's own header on SENTRY_BOX/SCAVENGER_BOX).
_frame: 4.27 x 4 tiles at TILE_SIZE 96. The cell is now PER-SLUG (M3 amended, 2026-08-12), and this slug is the one that is NOT 288: `packStrip`'s clipping check used to throw on the FIRST clipped frame, so its message reported that frame's own requirement and never evaluated the rest — that is how the record briefly read `death` needing 358 px (frame 4's figure). A full per-frame sweep (`tools/gen/sheets.mjs`, fixed to report the true maximum rather than the first hit) shows: walk 296, chase 273, death f0 170 f1 179 f2 243 f3 236 f4 358 f5 505 f6 507 f7 510 f8 508 f9 508 — MAX REQUIRED 510px at frame 7. 512 is chosen: 2px of spare over the true maximum, not the false 358.
_baseline: Same per-SHEET contact-frame rule as the courier's file (see character-bounds.json's `_baseline` note).

collisionBox._source: SCAVENGER_BOX x RENDER_SCALE (src/sim/enemyPlacement.ts:94). The ART is drawn narrower than this at the anchor, which is the safe direction, same as the courier's.

_stride: WALK MEASURED 2026-08-12 (session 7, work item D1), same foot-band method as the courier's file (see character-bounds.json's `_strideLevelledAnchor`): the widest foot-to-foot span at a contact frame is one step, doubled for the two steps in a cycle. Measured on the PACKED walk.png (384x384 cells, 12 frames) with a 24-game-px band above each frame's own deepest opaque row (robust to the per-frame lift 'feet' anchoring already applies): spans 121,153,156,134,98,66,63,62,69,127,46,45 across frames 0-11 — peaks at frame 2 (156) and frame 9 (127), troughs at frame 6/7 (63/62) and frame 10/11 (46/45). Two peaks and two troughs across the sheet independently confirm the sampler cut exactly one cycle, same as the courier's walk. Adopted the LARGER peak doubled (156 x 2 = 312), the same convention the courier's 127->254 and 160->320 entries used. CHASE IS INDETERMINATE, NOT measured, and must not be guessed: the same band swept at 16/24/32px shows only ONE peak and ONE trough across the 12-frame sheet (e.g. at 24px: 189,194,170,124,63,53,80,80,78,79,138,163 — a single rise-then-fall, not two), which is the courier's own run problem (vault 4.18) — the trailing leg is airborne at the fast gait's contact frames, so the foot band cannot call a second step. Its packed chase.png was therefore NOT shipped (deleted after measurement) rather than left as a catalog-less orphan; re-derive when a clip with two clean contact frames exists. ⚠️ Also carries the caveat already recorded in `_scale` above: the slug's 0.56074766 scale came from a GAIT, not a neutral pose (4.2% spread vs the sentry's 0.3%), so this stride must be re-derived if `walk` is ever re-shot.
_animations: ['walk','chase','death'] — must equal configFor('rust-scavenger').actions in tools/gen/slugConfig.mjs and ANIMS_BY_SLUG['rust-scavenger'] in src/render/enemyView.ts. There is no `idle`: the scavenger patrols continuously (src/render/enemyView.ts's `scavengerAnim`), so a standing pose is never reached and a sheet for it would be money spent on a state the sim cannot enter. `verticalAnchor` is 'feet' for all three: the scavenger never leaves the ground, same reasoning as the sentry's file.
_activeFrames: Empty for every animation. The scavenger has no attack state — its BODY is the hazard (contact damage, no swing, src/render/enemyView.ts's header) — so there is no strike window to align a per-frame hitbox against for this slug.
_loopFps: AUTHORED locomotion cadence (session 9), replacing stridePxPerCycle as the timing input for walk/chase. Full reasoning is in character-bounds.json _loopFps. walk 12 frames @ 18fps = 1.5 cycles/sec (the same cadence the player walk now uses, and the sibling project walkF uses); chase 12 @ 30 = 2.5 cycles/sec, a visibly quicker gait than the patrol. SNAPPED (session 9, second pass): cadenceTicks now rounds the TICKS PER FRAME, so an authored fps is served as the nearest cadence that holds every frame for a whole number of 60Hz refreshes -- walk 18 -> 3 ticks/frame = 20 fps, chase 30 -> 2 ticks/frame = 30 fps. chase was authored 24, which rounds to the SAME 3 ticks/frame as walk and would have made the two gaits identical on screen; 30 is the next value up and keeps chase visibly quicker. See tests/unit/loop-dwell.test.ts for why unevenly-held frames read as ghosting. STARTING POINTS, to be tuned by eye against the running character -- that is the point of authoring them. This also UNBLOCKS chase: it could never be catalogued before because its stride was unmeasured and catalogTimings threw rather than guess a number. A loop does not need a stride any more.
